% ---- Step 2: add to the Table 1 (tab:cells) caption
Abstention uses the 387-question sample; entropy is the mean over every pool question in the cell ($n=87$, 1{,}179, 676 and 361 for obscure known, obscure unknown, popular known and popular unknown).

% ---- Step 3: add to Questions & Labels, after the sentence with 2,303
Two questions with an empty subject were removed.

% ---- Step 4 / Prompt template (A3): design section
Knowledge is labelled under a forced-answer prompt and abstention under a free prompt. A gold alias appears in 0.98 of free replies in the popular known cell, 0.25 in the obscure known cell (0.53 if aliases that are part of the subject's name count), 0.37 in the popular unknown cell and 0.01 in the obscure unknown cell (post hoc). In 26 of the 87 obscure known questions a gold answer is part of the name, so the first two figures are close to a lower and an upper bound; on the other 61 the share is 0.33 [0.23, 0.44].

% ---- Headline template (A5)
Among questions the model cannot answer, abstention is higher for obscure than for popular entities: $+0.34$ [$+0.25$, $+0.43$] raw and $+0.18$ [$+0.04$, $+0.31$] after three label corrections (post hoc; 81 obscure and 39 popular questions remain). Resampling relations gives [$+0.22$, $+0.46$] and [$+0.03$, $+0.34$]; resampling relations and then questions gives [$+0.20$, $+0.48$] and [$-0.01$, $+0.37$].

% ---- Margin template (A1, A6)
Over all questions, popularity's effect ($+0.39$) exceeds knowledge's ($+0.09$), a margin of $+0.30$ [$+0.20$, $+0.40$]; resampling relations widens the interval to [$-0.09$, $+0.43$]. Within relations the mean margin depends on how many questions a relation must have in every cell: $+0.21$ [$+0.11$, $+0.30$] with at least one (six relations), $-0.04$ [$-0.20$, $+0.11$] with three (country, composer, sport) and $+0.24$ [$+0.02$, $+0.44$] with five (country, sport; regex, full pool, post hoc). The overall pattern therefore does not identify which factor matters more.

% (the paper's relation interval is [-0.10, +0.43] from 5,000 draws; 10,000 draws give -0.09. Monte Carlo only: use one of them throughout)

% ---- Judges template (A4, A9)
% NOTE: the plan's '[A4 one-judge]' slot is NOT the +0.13. They differ in replies, prompt and correction; both are stated.
The primary measure counts a reply as an abstention only when both judges agree ($\kappa=0.62$ [0.57, 0.67]). On the same 96-token replies the margin is $+0.44$ with Qwen2.5-32B alone, $+0.26$ with Gemma-2-27B alone and $+0.43$ with the regex. The earlier judge-corrected measure ($+0.13$) used the same Qwen judge on 24-token replies with a two-way prompt, which put popular unknown abstention at 0.57 rather than 0.22; reply length and prompt changed together, so their separate effects are not known.

% ---- Post hoc template (A10)
The two-judge measure was specified in writing before it was run, but after the one-judge result had been seen (Table~\ref{tab:x0choices}).

% ---- Step 7 (A7)
% NOTE: the plan's sentence ('abstention tracks popularity more than entropy') holds only across the two arms; see the last two clauses.
Across the 2,303 questions, regex abstention changes by $-0.26$ [$-0.27$, $-0.24$] per standard deviation of log page views and $+0.18$ [$+0.16$, $+0.19$] per standard deviation of entropy; among known facts, $-0.19$ and $+0.03$ (post hoc). The difference in size is $+0.08$, with a relation-resampled interval of [$-0.02$, $+0.16$], and it reflects a design that samples only the extreme tenths of page views: within each popularity group entropy is the larger predictor (obscure $-0.03$ vs.\ $+0.12$; popular $-0.05$ vs.\ $+0.13$).

% ---- Step 8 (A8): Limitations
% NOTE: replaces '1 in 12 unstable'. That figure is arithmetic (14 of 87 facts are 9/10) and the unknown 100% is true by construction.

The known label is fragile. 14 of the 87 obscure known facts sit exactly at the 9-of-10 cut-off; random halves of the stored samples return the stored label for 92\% of obscure known and 97\% of popular known facts, the rest falling in the dropped band. Under a paraphrased prompt only 27 of 87 obscure known facts (31\%) stay known, 49 fall in the dropped band and 11 become unknown; unknown labels are steadier (obscure 98\%, popular 71\%). On freshly sampled answers to the same prompt, 99\% of obscure and 92\% of popular unknown facts stay unknown. At a 10-of-10 cut-off the margin is $+0.28$ [$+0.17$, $+0.38$].

% ---- Limitations (human validation, prompt gap, concentration)
Neither the judges nor the regex were validated against human labels. Knowledge is labelled under a forced-answer prompt but abstention is measured under a free one. Of the 87 obscure known facts, 80 come from three relations (country 46, capital 27, sport 7), so the known-fact comparison rests on those.

% ---- Design / appendix: what 'corrected' means (two different corrections in the paper; name them apart)
\emph{Judge-corrected abstention} (the $+0.13$ row): in each cell, $\hat r = r\,p + (1-r)\,m$, where $r$ is the regex abstention rate over the cell's 24-token replies, $p$ the share of regex-positive replies that Qwen2.5-32B calls an abstention, and $m$ the share of regex-negative ones it does. $p$ and $m$ come from 50 judged replies per stratum ($r$, $p$, $m$ in popular unknown: 0.24, 1.00, 0.44). \emph{Label-corrected} results (the $+0.18$ gap, the $+0.14$ margin) instead change the knowledge labels: unknown facts are regraded by meaning with Llama-3.3-70B, popular unknown questions with the gold answer in any free reply are dropped, and guessable facts are dropped.
\emph{Third judge.} Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (4-bit, greedy), same prompt as the other two; a reply abstains if at least two of three say DONT\_KNOW (pre-specified; no tie is possible).
\emph{Settings.} Three replies per question, temperature 0.7, 96 new tokens, seed 0; judges greedy. Intervals in this appendix: 95\% percentile bootstrap, 10,000 resamples, seed 0, resampling questions within cells, or whole relations (all 16 drawn with replacement; resamples with an empty cell dropped). Elsewhere in the paper relation resampling and the judge correction use 5,000 resamples, and the linear probability models 2,000.
\emph{Relations.} author, capital, capital of, color, composer, country, director, father, genre, mother, occupation, place of birth, producer, religion, screenwriter, sport.
\emph{Popularity.} PopQA's \texttt{s\_pop}, documented as monthly Wikipedia page views; the dataset card and the PopQA paper do not state the month.
\emph{Compute.} One 24\,GB GPU for the 7--9B models; 45--65\,GB for the 27--32B and 70B (4-bit) judges.
\emph{Licences.} PopQA code repository: MIT (the dataset card states none). Llama-3.1 and Llama-3.3: Llama Community Licences; Gemma-2: Gemma terms; Qwen2.5-7B/32B, Mistral-7B-v0.3 and OLMo-2-7B: Apache-2.0. Our code: MIT. Code: [ANONYMISED LINK].
